German Industrials Hit by 2019 Cyberattack: Sector Recounts Lasting Lessons

In June 2019, Germany’s diversified industrials sector faced its most serious cyber incident to date when a coordinated ransomware attack disrupted operations across multiple firms, highlighting vulnerabilities in the backbone of the nation’s manufacturing economy.

The attack, believed by investigators to have originated with the infection of a widely used software update platform, struck at least 11 companies, including leading players such as Nordwerk AG and the mid-sized conglomerate HesseMachinery GmbH. Production lines in North Rhine-Westphalia and Baden-Württemberg came to a standstill as IT systems were locked down, with ransom demands delivered in encrypted messages.

“Within an hour, our entire ERP system was inaccessible,” recalled Dr. Klaus Weber, Chief Information Officer of Nordwerk AG. “We had to switch to manual processes for everything from logistics to payroll. It was chaos.” The German Association of Industrial Producers (VdIP) estimated that the sector lost approximately €180 million in output over two weeks, with full restoration of system functionality taking up to a month for some firms.

While no confidential customer data was publicly leaked, several companies reported delays in fulfilling export orders and temporary furloughs for hundreds of workers. “The attack exposed how tightly integrated our operational technology is with our digital infrastructure,” said Anke Ritter, spokesperson for the IG Metall union. “Employees faced uncertainty, and trust in digitalisation suffered a blow.”

The Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) led the investigation, confirming that the ransomware exploited an unpatched vulnerability in a legacy third-party component. “This incident demonstrated the need for sector-wide cyber hygiene and continuous patch management,” said BSI President Arne Vogt.

Since 2019, the affected firms have overhauled their cybersecurity protocols, investing in real-time monitoring, employee training, and secure software supply chains. “The attack was a wake-up call,” said Weber. “It forced us to rethink resilience at every level of operation.”

Though the immediate disruptions of 2019 have long since passed, industry representatives stress that vigilance remains paramount. “The lessons of that summer continue to shape our approach to risk,” said Ritter.
